title: Taxpayer-Funded Pro-Trump Ads Spark Criticism Ahead of Midterms
summary:
With the U.S. midterm elections just weeks away, the White House is spending taxpayer money on television ads that look and sound like campaign commercials for President Donald Trump. The ads have appeared in prime timeslots, including during NFL games last weekend, and have cost at least $1.4 million so far, according to AdImpact, an advertising tracking firm.

The White House defends the ads as 'public service announcements' that are 'unapologetically American.' A spokesperson said, 'The announcements are very clearly not campaign ads. President Trump is not on the ballot and there is no call to action.' It is true that Trump is not up for re-election on November 3, but he did tell the audience at this month's Republican convention to 'pretend that I'm on the ballot' — an effort to boost turnout for Republican candidates in tight House and Senate races.

Criticism has come from both sides. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a Republican, told reporters on Capitol Hill, 'I like the message, but it shouldn't be paid for by taxpayer dollars.' Democratic lawmakers sent a letter to Trump's chief of staff calling the ads 'government propaganda' and 'an egregious and utterly illegal misuse of Americans' hard-earned tax dollars.' One ad features a choir singing 'Love Me' over photos of Trump, while another is nearly identical to a 2024 Trump campaign ad. The funding comes from U.S. Customs and Border Protection, an agency of the Department of Homeland Security, according to the Wall Street Journal.

The 'Love Me' ad opens with grainy black-and-white video of Trump saying, 'Together we will defeat communism, socialism and Marxism in America.' It then flashes slides reading 'Largest Tax Cuts in History' and 'Reigniting American Manufacturing,' and ends with Trump standing beside Dana White, CEO of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, as the words 'Paid for by the U.S. Government' appear on screen. Another ad uses clips from Trump's July 3 speech at Mount Rushmore, where he says, 'We are the freest people on earth.'

The controversy raises a key question: should public money be used to promote a political leader? With Trump's approval rating at an all-time low and control of Congress at stake, the answer could shape the midterm elections.
why_it_matters: This goes beyond one election: it tests where the line sits between a government informing the public and a government promoting the person in power, and the answer sets a precedent for how official communication is used in the future.

background_read: U.S. midterm elections happen every two years in early November, when all 435 House seats and about a third of the Senate are decided. They are widely treated as a verdict on the sitting president even though the president's own name is not on the ballot.

Federal rules generally bar agencies from spending money Congress appropriated on publicity or propaganda designed to influence elections — a principle policed by the Government Accountability Office (the nonpartisan watchdog that reviews how federal money is spent) and by Congress itself.

The money here comes from U.S. Customs and Border Protection, part of the Department of Homeland Security (the cabinet department created after the September 11 attacks to coordinate border, immigration and security agencies) — an agency whose usual job is border enforcement, not messaging.

One ad ends with Trump beside Dana White (the CEO of the Ultimate Fighting Championship, a major mixed martial arts company), while another uses clips from a speech at Mount Rushmore (a national memorial in South Dakota where the faces of four U.S. presidents are carved into a granite cliff).

Because Trump told a Republican convention audience to 'pretend that I'm on the ballot,' critics argue the ads function as campaign material even though the White House insists there is no call to action.

perspectives.perspective: The White House and its defenders
perspectives.description: They argue the spots are ordinary public service announcements about tax cuts and manufacturing, paid for by an agency with its own communications budget. Because Trump is not on the ballot and the ads contain no explicit call to vote, they say the comparison to campaign commercials is a partisan attack.

Democratic lawmakers call the ads 'government propaganda' and an illegal misuse of tax dollars, while Republican Senator John Thune objects that taxpayers should not fund them even if he likes the message. The concern is that public money is being converted into an incumbency advantage at the moment voters are deciding who controls Congress.

Watchdogs note that governments have long blurred the line between informing the public and promoting the people in charge, and that the legal rules against publicly funded 'publicity or propaganda' are vague and rarely enforced. The unusual part here is the scale, the prime-time placement, and funding routed through a border agency rather than a communications office.

If the ads go unchallenged, future administrations of both parties may treat them as a normal tool of government messaging; if Congress or the courts intervene, new limits could follow. Either way, this episode is likely to be cited as a precedent whenever public money and political messaging mix.
